newsitem.title: USA: Sears to tread more lightly with deadbeats.
newsitem.headline: Sears to tread more lightly with deadbeats.

text.p: Sears, Roebuck & Co. has agreed to stop using idle threats with consumers to recoup credit card debt, and the change is expected to put a drag on the retailer's profits, experts said Thursday.

By toning down the way it negotiates so-called reaffirmation agreements with credit card customers, Sears could lose between 5 cents and 10 cents a share in future annual earnings, analysts said. The company earned $1.3 billion, or $3.12 a share, in 1996.

Sears, the nation's second-largest retailer, agreed a week ago to pay between $178 million and $265 million to settle claims that its methods of collecting debt from credit card consumers in bankruptcy cases was illegal.
In the past, Sears used threats of taking back merchandise as a stick to prod Sears charge card customers to enter agreements to pay off debt after bankruptcy.

"Sears can't make threats to repossess merchandise where it does not have a legal right or a present intention to repossess the goods," said Christopher Barry-Smith, an attorney with the Massachusetts Attorney General's office. "They can't intimidate debtors with empty threats."

In the future, Sears is expected to limit its repossession warnings to cases where consumers made big-ticket purchases, including washing machines, sofas or big-screen TVs. It also has pledged to file the repayment agreements in court, which is required by law.

"In the case of clothing or end tables or lamps, they obviously wouldn't ever go out and repossess those items," said Michaela White, a Creighton University law professor who has studied reaffirmation agreements and bankruptcy codes.
That means many consumers who made small purchases will have less incentive to enter repayment agreements in the future.
On the other hand, Sears still can offer to extend fresh credit on the Sears charge card as a carrot to customers who pay off their old debt.
"A lot of people view Sears as an old friend," White said. "The incentive of new credit may be enough" to get them to enter a reaffirmation pact.
Sears has 60 million charge card customers, and about 31 million used their Sears card in the last 12 months.

Between 1992 and 1997, customers owing Sears $2.4 billion filed for bankruptcy protection. Of that, about $400 million was subject to reaffirmation agreements. Of that, Sears figured it improperly collected between $90 million and $160 million and has agreed to refund it.
Collection of bad debt has been just one factor nudging earnings at the retailer's credit operaton, experts noted. The rate of delinquencies and bankruptcies has been another.

Bankruptcy filings by consumers hit a record 1.1 million in 1996, and the tidal wave could swell to 1.35 million this year, predicted Stuart Feldstein, president of SMR Research Corp., a financial services research firm.
Sears already has changed the way it negotiates reaffirmation agreements. But Chairman and Chief Executive Arthur Martinez said it was too early to tell how it will influence the bottom line.

"I think it's reasonable to expect there will be an impact," he said last week. "It will take a few months of experience for us in the new mode, which we really commenced the first of April, to get enough experience to know what kind of reaffirmation rate we can reasonably expect."

So far, the mishap apparently has not tarnished the company's reputation, said Dillon, Read & Co. analyst Peter Schaeffer. A poll of consumers by Sears showed zero to 2 percent had heard of the controversy.
Sears' stock was up 87.5 cents at $53.75 on the New York Stock Exchange in late trading.
